tiles.title: Comparison and Logical Operators
tiles.summary: Learn Python's arithmetic, comparison and logical operators, understand short-circuit evaluation and operator priority, and convert values between int, float and str.

steps.title: Seven operators for numeric work
steps.lede: Python gives you seven arithmetic operators — including two you may not have seen before.

blocks.text: Python provides seven arithmetic operators for numeric work. The familiar four — + (addition), - (subtraction), * (multiplication) and / (division) — work as expected, but / always returns a float even when both operands are whole numbers: 8 / 2 gives 4.0, not 4. The ** operator raises a number to a power: 5 ** 2 is 25.

The // operator performs floor division: it divides and discards the fractional part, so 17 // 5 is 3. The % operator returns the remainder of the division, so 17 % 5 is 2. Together they let you split a quantity into whole units and a leftover — for example, 17 minutes is 3 complete five-minute slots with 2 minutes remaining.

Parentheses group an expression and control the order of evaluation: (32 + 8) * 2 adds first, then multiplies, giving 80. When an expression mixes an int and a float, Python converts the integer to floating point before computing — so 4 * 3.75 - 1 evaluates to 14.0, not 14.

right.code:
(32 + 8) * 2    # parentheses group first
4 * 3.75 - 1    # int promoted to float

annotations.text: Result: 80 — parentheses force addition before multiplication

blocks.takeaway: 17 // 5 is 3 and 17 % 5 is 2; parentheses control evaluation order; mixing int and float promotes the result to float.

steps.title: Six operators that return True or False
steps.lede: Comparisons turn a question about data into a boolean value Python can branch on.

blocks.text: Comparing two values is how a question like 'is this delivery late?' becomes something Python can act on. The six comparison operators are < (less than), <= (less than or equal), > (greater than), >= (greater than or equal), == (equal) and != (not equal). Every comparison evaluates to exactly one of the two boolean values: True or False.

annotations.text: True for any city other than Lagos

blocks.takeaway: Each operator returns True or False; delivery_minutes > 60 is True for a 72-minute order and False for a 32-minute one.

steps.title: Combining conditions with and, or and not
steps.lede: Build compound conditions from simpler comparisons using Python's three logical operators.

blocks.text: A single comparison asks one question at a time. To combine conditions — 'is this delivery both late and far from the depot?' — Python provides three logical operators: or, and and not. In ascending priority order they are: or (lowest), and, not (highest among the three). When there are no parentheses, and binds more tightly than or.

x or y returns x if x is true, otherwise y. It is short-circuit: if is_late is True, Python never evaluates is_far. x and y returns x if x is false, otherwise y. It is also short-circuit: if is_late is False, Python skips is_far entirely.

left.code:
is_late or is_far
True or False
False or True
False or False

right.code:
is_late and is_far
True and True
True and False
False and True

annotations.text: True only if both conditions hold

blocks.takeaway: or is true when at least one operand is true; and is true only when both are; both short-circuit to skip the second operand when the result is already determined.

steps.title: not, priority and real-world compound conditions
steps.lede: not flips a boolean; priority rules determine how mixed expressions group without parentheses.

blocks.text: not x flips the boolean: not is_late is True when is_late is False, and False when is_late is True. not has lower priority than the comparison operators, so not delivery_minutes == 0 is read as not (delivery_minutes == 0), not as (not delivery_minutes) == 0.

A rule like 'flag this delivery if it is late or unusually far' reads directly as is_late or is_far. A stricter rule — 'flag it only if it is late and it is the driver's first week' — reads as is_late and is_first_week. and, or and not let you build one compound condition out of several simpler comparisons.

steps.title: Converting between strings and numbers
steps.lede: int(), float() and str() let you move values between types — but only when the format matches.

blocks.text: Data often arrives as the wrong type. A delivery time typed into a form as the text '32' cannot be used in arithmetic until it is converted to a number. Python provides three constructors for explicit conversion: int() and float() produce a number from a string or another numeric type, and str() turns any value into its string representation.

int('123') returns the integer 123. float('+1.23') returns the float 1.23. str(32) turns the integer 32 into the string '32'. These conversions work in both directions between numbers and their string representations.

Not every string can be converted. float() requires the string to match a numeric format — an optional sign, digits, and optionally a decimal point or exponent — after stripping surrounding whitespace. int() requires an integer string. A string that does not match raises a ValueError: int('3.5') fails because '3.5' is not an integer string.

annotations.text: String '32' — cannot add a number to it
TypeError: can only concatenate str to str

blocks.change_summary: Converting '32' from string to int with int() makes arithmetic possible; without conversion, adding a number raises a TypeError.

steps.title: What you learned
steps.lede: Key ideas from this tile.

blocks.text: Comparison operators (<, <=, >, >=, ==, !=) each return True or False. and, or and not combine those booleans into compound conditions; and has higher priority than or. Converting a string to a number only works when the string matches the format the target type accepts — otherwise the conversion raises a ValueError.

remediation_steps.lede: A clear contrast showing how parentheses change the result, and why mixing int and float gives a float.

blocks.text: Parentheses control evaluation order: (32 + 8) * 2 adds first, giving 80. Without parentheses, * runs before +. When you mix an int and a float in one operation, Python promotes the int to float: 4 * 3.75 - 1 gives 14.0, not 14.

blocks.change_summary: Adding parentheses changes the evaluation order and the result.

remediation_steps.title: Comparison operators and boolean results
remediation_steps.lede: A side-by-side contrast showing the same expression returning different booleans for different values.

blocks.text: The six comparison operators are < (less than), <= (less than or equal), > (greater than), >= (greater than or equal), == (equal) and != (not equal). Every comparison returns exactly True or False — never a number.

blocks.takeaway: The same expression delivery_minutes > 60 gives False for 32 and True for 72.

remediation_steps.title: Operator priority: and before or
remediation_steps.lede: A contrast showing how and and or group when there are no parentheses.

blocks.text: In ascending priority order the logical operators are: or (lowest), and, not. and binds more tightly than or, so is_late or is_far and is_first_week groups as is_late or (is_far and is_first_week). not has lower priority than comparison operators: not delivery_minutes == 0 means not (delivery_minutes == 0).

annotations.text: Groups as: is_late or (is_far and is_first_week)
Parentheses override priority — both sides must be true

blocks.change_summary: Without parentheses, and groups first; adding parentheses changes which conditions must both be true.

remediation_steps.title: Short-circuit evaluation in or and and
remediation_steps.lede: A side-by-side contrast showing when each operator stops evaluating early.

blocks.text: or short-circuits: if the first operand is True, Python returns it immediately without evaluating the second. and short-circuits: if the first operand is False, Python returns it immediately without evaluating the second. This means is_late or is_far only checks is_far when is_late is False, and is_late and is_far only checks is_far when is_late is True.

blocks.takeaway: Both operators skip the second operand when the first operand already determines the result.

remediation_steps.lede: A before/after showing what happens with and without int().

blocks.text: int('123') returns 123. float('+1.23') returns 1.23. str(32) returns '32'. These constructors convert between compatible types: a string of digits to int, a numeric-format string to float, any value to its string form.

blocks.change_summary: Wrapping '32' in int() converts it to the integer 32, making arithmetic possible.

remediation_steps.title: When type conversion raises ValueError
remediation_steps.lede: A contrast between a failing conversion and a working alternative.

blocks.text: float() requires the string to match a numeric format: an optional sign, digits, and optionally a decimal point or exponent, after stripping surrounding whitespace. int() requires an integer string — no decimal point. A string that does not match raises a ValueError: int('3.5') fails because '3.5' contains a decimal point.

annotations.text: ValueError — '3.5' is not an integer string
Result: 3.5 — decimal strings are valid for float()

blocks.takeaway: int() cannot parse a decimal string — it raises ValueError. float() accepts decimal strings; use float() when the string contains a decimal point.

tiles.title: Lists, Dictionaries, and Tuples
tiles.summary: Store ordered sequences in lists, map keys to values in dictionaries, and group fixed records in immutable tuples.

steps.title: Ordered, mutable sequences
steps.lede: A list stores an ordered sequence of values you can index, slice and modify.

blocks.text: Keeping five separate variables for five delivery times gets unwieldy fast. A list stores an ordered sequence of values in a single name: delivery_times = [32, 45, 21, 60, 18]. Items are indexed from 0 at the left and from -1 at the right, so delivery_times[0] is 32 and delivery_times[-1] is 18.

A slice extracts a sub-list: delivery_times[1:3] returns [45, 21]. The start index is included; the end index is excluded. delivery_times[-3:] returns the last three items. Lists are mutable: delivery_times[3] = 64 replaces the item at index 3 in place.

steps.title: Key-to-value lookup
steps.lede: A dictionary maps unique keys to values — look up a city by order ID, not by position.

blocks.text: Sometimes you need to look up a value by a meaningful key rather than by position. A dictionary is a collection of key: value pairs written inside braces, where keys must be unique: order_city = {1042: 'Lagos', 1043: 'Abuja', 1044: 'Kano'}. Retrieve a value by subscripting with its key: order_city[1042] returns 'Lagos'.

Store or update a value by assigning to a key: order_city[1044] = 'Kano' adds a new entry; assigning to an existing key replaces its value. The get() method returns None (or a specified default) instead of raising an error when a key is absent: order_city.get(9999) returns None rather than crashing.
Subscripting a key that is not in the dictionary raises a KeyError: order_city[9999] fails if no order 9999 was ever added. Use get() when you are not certain the key exists.

steps.title: Immutable sequences and unpacking
steps.lede: A tuple groups a fixed set of values; unpacking hands each piece back to its own name.

blocks.text: A tuple groups a small, fixed set of values together. It is written as comma-separated values, with or without surrounding parentheses: order = 1042, 'Lagos', 32 or order = (1042, 'Lagos', 32). Python shows tuples enclosed in parentheses on output.

Tuples are immutable: once created, an item cannot be reassigned. order[0] = 1099 raises a TypeError. Also, enclosing a single value in parentheses does not make it a tuple — singleton = ('Lagos') is still just the string 'Lagos'. A one-item tuple needs a trailing comma: singleton = 'Lagos',

annotations.text: Three values packed into one tuple

blocks.change_summary: Unpacking hands each element of the tuple back to its own name — order_id, city and minutes are now separate variables.

steps.title: What you learned
steps.lede: Key ideas from this tile.

blocks.text: A list is an ordered, mutable sequence indexed from 0; slices use start-included, end-excluded bounds; index assignment replaces an item in place and append() adds one at the end. A dictionary maps unique keys to values; subscripting a missing key raises a KeyError — use get() to avoid it. A tuple groups a fixed set of values that cannot be reassigned; unpacking distributes each element to its own name.

tiles.title: Sets and Strings
tiles.summary: Use sets to collect unique values and test membership, combine sets with union and intersection, and build readable messages with f-strings and format specifiers.

steps.title: Unique, unordered collections
steps.lede: A set stores only distinct values — duplicates are automatically removed.

blocks.text: Sometimes you only care about which distinct values appear — which cities orders were delivered to, with no duplicates. A set is an unordered collection with no duplicate elements, used for membership testing and eliminating duplicate entries.

Curly braces or the set() function create a set. set() must be used for an empty set, because {} creates an empty dictionary instead. set() can also build a set from another collection: cities = set(['Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Lagos', 'Kano']) produces {'Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Kano'} — the duplicate 'Lagos' is collapsed to one entry.

blocks.change_summary: Passing the list through set() collapses the repeated 'Lagos' to a single entry, leaving only unique cities.

blocks.text: Test whether a value is in the set with the `in` operator: `'Lagos' in cities` returns `True` if `'Lagos'` is in the set, and `False` otherwise. This membership test is the primary reason to use a set rather than a list when you only need to check presence.

steps.title: Union and intersection
steps.lede: | combines two sets; & finds what they share.

blocks.text: Set objects support mathematical operations. Union (a | b) gives all elements from both sets. Intersection (a & b) gives only elements present in both: week1_cities & week2_cities gives cities that appeared in both weeks.

steps.title: Embedding values and formatting numbers
steps.lede: f-strings embed variable values directly in a string; a format specifier controls how numbers are displayed.

blocks.text: A quote character can be embedded in a string without escaping it by using the other kind of quote. Writing "This delivery wasn't late" inside double quotes needs no escaping; the same text inside single quotes would need the apostrophe escaped as \'.

An f-string is a string literal prefixed with f or F that embeds the value of a Python expression inside the string by writing the expression in curly brackets: f"Delivery to {city} took {delivery_minutes} minutes" substitutes in the current values of city and delivery_minutes.

An optional format specifier follows the expression after a colon, controlling how the value is displayed. f"Average: {avg_minutes:.2f} minutes" produces 'Average: 32.67 minutes' when avg_minutes is 32.666 — the .2f specifier rounds to two decimal places.

blocks.change_summary: Adding :.2f after the expression rounds the output to two decimal places — the {value:.2f} part and its rounded result.

steps.lede: Key ideas from this tile.

blocks.text: A set stores only distinct values — pass a list through set() to remove duplicates. The in operator tests membership; | and & compute union and intersection. f-strings embed variable values with {expression}; a format specifier like :.2f controls decimal places.

remediation_steps.title: Creating a set and removing duplicates
remediation_steps.lede: A before/after showing how set() collapses duplicates from a list.

blocks.text: A set is an unordered collection with no duplicate elements. Use set() to create one from a list: set(['Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Lagos', 'Kano']) gives {'Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Kano'}. Use {} for a non-empty set literal: {'Lagos', 'Abuja'}. For an empty set, you must use set() — {} creates an empty dictionary.

blocks.change_summary: Converting the list to a set removes the duplicate 'Lagos', reducing the count from 4 to 3.

remediation_steps.title: Union and intersection on sets
remediation_steps.lede: A side-by-side contrast showing | and & on the same two sets.

blocks.text: | (union) gives all elements from either set — no duplicates. & (intersection) gives only the elements present in both sets. If week1_cities = {'Lagos', 'Abuja'} and week2_cities = {'Abuja', 'Kano'}, then week1_cities | week2_cities is {'Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Kano'} and week1_cities & week2_cities is {'Abuja'}.

blocks.takeaway: | combines both sets; & keeps only what they have in common.

remediation_steps.title: Embedding a quote without escaping
remediation_steps.lede: A side-by-side contrast showing the same string with and without an escape.

blocks.text: A quote character can be embedded in a string without escaping it by enclosing the string in the other kind of quote. "This delivery wasn't late" uses double quotes, so the apostrophe in wasn't needs no backslash. Inside single quotes the same apostrophe would need escaping: 'This delivery wasn\'t late'.

annotations.text: No backslash needed — double quotes wrap the string

blocks.takeaway: Switching to the other kind of quote avoids the need to escape the embedded quote character.
